explanations.explanation: That's the word, friend. The crowd took palm branches and went out to meet Him (John 12:13). Nobody is sneaking around here. They head out with branches in their hands and a whole lot of shouting.

I get why warn crossed your mind, because a crowd with sticks can sound like trouble. But the text says they took palm branches and went out to meet Him (John 12:13). Nothing about a warning. Then they start shouting “Hosanna!” and that is not warning talk.

Stop is a fair guess if you picture a crowd blocking the road. But John 12:13 says they took palm branches and went out to meet Him. Then they shout, “Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord!” That is not how you greet someone you want to stop.

True, friend. Along with “Hosanna!” and “Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord!” they shout, “Blessed is the King of Israel!” (John 12:13). That's three shouts from one crowd. This crowd was not holding anything back.

It's true, actually. The crowd shouts three things, and the last one is “Blessed is the King of Israel!” (John 12:13). So the King part is right there in the shouting. Easy one to miss when the first two shouts are so loud.

Yes, friend. John says Jesus sat on the young donkey “…as it is written…” (John 12:14). So this was no random pick. Scripture already had a word about it, and John points right to it in the next verse.

The crowd took palm branches and went out shouting, but John never says they asked for a donkey (John 12:13). He says Jesus sat on it “…as it is written…” (John 12:14). The thing behind it is what was written, not what anyone asked for.

That makes sense if you picture the disciples organizing the whole parade. But the text never says they planned anything. John says Jesus sat on the donkey “…as it is written…” (John 12:14). He also says the disciples did not understand these things at first (John 12:16), so I think a plan from them is a stretch.

That's it, friend. The words begin, “Do not be afraid, O Daughter of Zion.” (John 12:15). Then they go on, “See, your King is coming, seated on the colt of a donkey.” The very first thing said to her is not to fear.

Battle is a natural guess when a king is coming. But the words say, “Do not be afraid, O Daughter of Zion.” (John 12:15). Nothing in them calls for a fight. Just a King, seated on the colt of a donkey.

Hiding would be the opposite of what these words say. They tell her, “Do not be afraid, O Daughter of Zion.” (John 12:15). Then they say, “See, your King is coming…” See means look, not duck behind the couch.

Not quite. John says, “At first His disciples did not understand these things…” (John 12:16). The understanding came later, so right away is the part that doesn't fit. Good news is that later did arrive.

Right, friend. John says, “At first His disciples did not understand these things…” (John 12:16). They stood in the middle of it all and still didn't get it. Then they came to understand, which is the next part of the verse.

You got it, baker. John says the people who were with Jesus when He called Lazarus from the tomb “…continued to testify.” (John 12:17). They had seen it, and they kept on telling it. That kind of story doesn't stay in one place.

That's the opposite of what John says. These people “…continued to testify.” (John 12:17). They saw Jesus call Lazarus out of the tomb, and they kept talking about it. Testify means telling, not tucking away.

John doesn't say anything about them asking for more. He says they “…continued to testify.” (John 12:17). Their job here was telling what they had already seen. The crowd then goes out to meet Jesus because they heard about that sign (John 12:18).

True, friend. John says, “That is also why the crowd went out to meet Him, because they heard that He had performed this sign.” (John 12:18). The sign is Lazarus coming out of the tomb. The word spread, and the crowd came.

This one is true. John says the crowd went out to meet Him “…because they heard that He had performed this sign.” (John 12:18). The sign is the raising of Lazarus from the dead. That's what got the crowd moving.

Close, but no. The Pharisees say to one another, “You can see that this is doing you no good.” (John 12:19). That is not a group saying things are going well. I think they were watching the crowd go after Jesus and weren't happy about it.

Yes, friend. The Pharisees tell one another, “You can see that this is doing you no good. Look how the whole world has gone after Him!” (John 12:19). So they say it's not going well for them. That's their own way of putting it, and they say it out loud to each other.
